mcqs.question: What was the actual purpose of Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminating production instances during business hours?
options: To reduce cloud infrastructure costs by shutting down unused instances
To force engineers to build services that tolerate instance failure as a baseline expectation, tested on the team's own schedule rather than discovered during a real outage
To test the on-call rotation's paging system only
To identify which engineers were slowest to respond to alerts
mcqs.explanation: Chaos Monkey's point was making instance failure a routine, expected condition that services had to handle by design, verified proactively during business hours instead of being discovered for the first time during an uncontrolled production incident. It wasn't about cost-cutting, testing paging alone, or evaluating individual engineers.

mcqs.question: Why does a chaos experiment need an explicit steady-state hypothesis before injecting any failure?
options: It's a legal requirement for running experiments in production
Without a measurable baseline for "normal," there's nothing to compare against, so you can't objectively tell whether the system held up
It determines which team members are allowed to run the experiment
It's only needed for experiments run in staging, not production
mcqs.explanation: The hypothesis defines a measurable normal state (e.g. specific latency and error-rate thresholds), which is what turns "did the system hold up" into an objective, evidence-based answer rather than a subjective impression. It isn't a legal, staffing, or environment-specific requirement — it's what makes the experiment scientifically meaningful at all.

mcqs.question: What does responsible blast-radius control look like when starting a new chaos experiment?
options: Running the full experiment across all of production immediately to get realistic results
Starting at the smallest scale (staging, then a single instance, then a small traffic percentage) with an abort switch, and expanding scope only after confidence is earned
Only ever running experiments in staging, never in production
Skipping staging entirely since it never matches production traffic
mcqs.explanation: Blast radius should grow incrementally as confidence builds, always with the ability to abort immediately if things go worse than expected — jumping straight to full production risks turning the experiment into a real incident. Staying only in staging forever misses failure modes tied to real production traffic, so a graduated approach into production is typically necessary.

mcqs.question: What does a game day test that a narrow, automated single-fault chaos experiment typically doesn't?
options: Whether a specific microservice retries correctly on a dropped dependency
The whole incident-response process — paging, on-call runbooks, dashboards, and team communication — not just an isolated technical fault
Whether the CI pipeline builds successfully
The cloud provider's SLA compliance
mcqs.explanation: A game day simulates something closer to a real incident end-to-end, exercising the human and process side (paging, runbooks, communication, whether dashboards actually surface the right signal) that a narrow automated fault injection doesn't touch. It's not focused on a single service's retry logic, CI, or provider SLA terms.

mcqs.question: In the checkout example, why did injecting 3 seconds of latency reveal a real gap even though the service had a "reasonable timeout"?
options: Because the timeout value itself was set too high
Because a timeout without retry logic just turns a slow dependency into an outright failed request, which normal testing (which usually simulates fully-down, not slow, dependencies) hadn't caught
Because the payment provider was actually down, not just slow
Because the chaos tool itself was misconfigured
mcqs.explanation: The gap wasn't the timeout value — it was the missing retry behind it, so a merely slow (not fully down) dependency caused an immediate failure instead of a graceful retry. Standard testing rarely simulates a slow-but-alive dependency, which is exactly the blind spot the chaos experiment exposed.

mcqs.question: What's the actual fix for the risk of running chaos experiments in production?
options: Never run any chaos experiment in production, only in staging
Require every experiment to have an automated abort condition and a tested rollback plan before it runs, rather than avoiding production entirely
Only run experiments during off-peak hours with no other safeguards
Get executive sign-off before every single experiment
mcqs.explanation: Since staging often can't replicate real production traffic patterns, the practical fix is requiring a tested abort/rollback mechanism for every experiment rather than banning production experiments outright. Off-peak timing alone doesn't substitute for an abort mechanism, and executive sign-off addresses process, not the technical safety net.
